catalog_quote: 3.4 Suprasegmental Items 3.4.1 Stress, tone and length have not been observed to be pertinent Stress usually falls on the first syllable. /i/, /e/, /a/, /u/, and /u/, and /o/ have been observed to have greater intensity than /ə/. When /ə/ occurs in the first syllable and another vowel occurs in the following syllable, stress and length can move to the second syllable or both may have equal stress. ... 6 RESIDUE 6.1 Stress appears to become relevant with verbs. It appears to be contrastive in certain verbs, e.g.: [ə'ŋati] /ə'ŋati/ 'I bury a man' ['əŋati] /'əŋati/ 'I hurry' It is not known whether this only involves sentence stress or whether there is possibly an introduction of phonemic stress or length, or syllabic consonants.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both halves of the deciding quotation (p. 44 sec. 3.4.1 and p. 48 sec. 6.1) are verbatim in the held SIL scan at the stated PDF pages 16 and 20. (2) Deciding source: a 1977 SIL 'tentative phonemic statement' (phonology article, 20 pp) -- thin and self-described as tentative, but it is Glottolog's MED and the only phonological description of Yil anywhere I could verify (Glottolog JSON meds; SIL archive lists exactly two [yll] items; WALS cites only this). No grammar, sketch, dissertation, JIPA illustration or instrumental study exists to supersede it, so 'best available' is held. sources.quote: 'Stress is probably phonemic. Usually it falls on the first syllable, except when /ə/ occurs in the first syllable. This vowel tends to occur on unstressed syllables. There are contrastive pairs like: ə'ngati 'I bury a man' 'əngati 'I hurry'' (bibliography cites only Martens & Tuominen 1977).

sources.citation: No grammar, grammatical sketch or dissertation with interlinear glossed examples exists for Yil. Glottolog 5.3 lists 6 references for yill1241, MED = phonology (Martens & Tuominen 1977); the rest are Laycock overviews/wordlists (1968, 1973, notebook C5), Ethnologue and Glottolog itself.
